Test your knowledge of the material on [extending loglinear models](../lectures/08-Loglin2.pdf) in the following quiz to see how much you learned.
This is **entirely private for you**---no records are kept of your performance.

## Questions

**1. When one table variable is a binary response, a logit model for that response is:**

`r longmcq(c("More complex than the equivalent loglinear model",
             answer = "Equivalent to a loglinear model",
             "Unrelated to loglinear models",
             "Only valid for continuous predictors"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
Each logit model for a binary response C is equivalent to a loglinear model. The loglinear model must include the [AB] association of predictors. The logit model is simpler to interpret because it has fewer parameters and focuses on the effects on the response variable.
</div>

**2. The main advantage of the GLM (generalized linear model) approach to loglinear models is that GLM:**

`r longmcq(c("Only works with categorical predictors",
             "Requires larger sample sizes",
             answer = "Allows quantitative predictors and can handle ordinal factors",
             "Cannot handle overdispersion"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
The GLM approach allows quantitative predictors and special ways of treating ordinal factors. It provides parameter estimates with standard errors and significance tests, can incorporate ordinal variables as linear/polynomial terms, and can handle overdispersion using quasi-Poisson or negative binomial families.
</div>

**3. The linear-by-linear (L × L) model for ordinal variables assumes:**

`r longmcq(c("Different slopes for each category",
             answer = "A constant local odds ratio for adjacent categories",
             "No association between variables",
             "Only main effects, no interaction"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
The L × L model assumes log(m<sub>ij</sub>) = μ + λ<sub>i</sub><sup>A</sup> + λ<sub>j</sub><sup>B</sup> + γ a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>j</sub>, where γ is a constant local odds ratio. For integer scores, log(θ<sub>ij</sub>) = γ. This model uses only 1 more parameter than the independence model, making it very parsimonious.
</div>

**4. In models for ordered categories, the RC(1) model differs from the L × L model in that RC(1):**

`r longmcq(c("Uses more degrees of freedom",
             "Assumes independence",
             answer = "Estimates optimal row and column scores from the data",
             "Only applies to square tables"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
The RC(1) row-and-column effects model estimates optimal category scores α<sub>i</sub> and β<sub>j</sub> as parameters: λ<sub>ij</sub><sup>AB</sup> = γ α<sub>i</sub>β<sub>j</sub>. Unlike L × L which assigns fixed integer scores, RC(1) finds the best-fitting scores. The ordering and spacing of categories is estimated from the data, similar to correspondence analysis.
</div>

**5. For a square table with the same row and column categories, the quasi-independence model:**

`r longmcq(c("Assumes complete independence",
             answer = "Fits diagonal cells perfectly and tests independence in off-diagonal cells",
             "Requires equal marginal totals",
             "Only works with 2×2 tables"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
The quasi-independence model adds parameters δ<sub>i</sub> for each diagonal cell: log(m<sub>ij</sub>) = μ + λ<sub>i</sub><sup>A</sup> + λ<sub>j</sub><sup>B</sup> + δ<sub>i</sub>I(i=j). This fits the diagonal cells (where row = column) perfectly while testing for independence in the off-diagonal cells, which is useful for mobility tables and other square tables.
</div>

**6. The relationship between symmetry and quasi-symmetry models is:**

`r longmcq(c("They are identical models",
             "Symmetry is less restrictive than quasi-symmetry",
             answer = "Symmetry = quasi-symmetry + marginal homogeneity",
             "Quasi-symmetry always fits better than symmetry"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
For square tables, it can be shown that symmetry = quasi-symmetry + marginal homogeneity, and G²(S) = G²(QS) + G²(MH). The symmetry model assumes π<sub>ij</sub> = π<sub>ji</sub>, but this also implies marginal homogeneity (equal row and column totals). The quasi-symmetry model allows λ<sub>ij</sub> = λ<sub>ji</sub> without requiring equal margins.
</div>

**7. The gnm package in R is used to fit:**

`r longmcq(c("Only standard loglinear models",
             "Only logistic regression models",
             answer = "Generalized nonlinear models including RC and UNIDIFF models",
             "Only linear regression models"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
The gnm package provides functions to fit generalized nonlinear models (GNMs). RC models are not loglinear—they contain multiplicative terms like γ α<sub>i</sub>β<sub>j</sub>. The gnm() function can fit these models using Mult(), Exp(), and other nonlinear functions. The package also provides Diag(), Symm(), and Topo() convenience functions.
</div>

**8. In the UNIDIFF (uniform difference) model for stratified tables, the layer coefficients γ<sub>k</sub> represent:**

`r longmcq(c("The main effects of the layer variable",
             answer = "Multiplicative effects showing how association strength varies across layers",
             "The independence of layers",
             "Only the diagonal associations"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
The UNIDIFF model is log(m<sub>ijk</sub>) = μ + λ<sub>i</sub><sup>R</sup> + λ<sub>j</sub><sup>C</sup> + λ<sub>k</sub><sup>L</sup> + λ<sub>ik</sub><sup>RL</sup> + λ<sub>jk</sub><sup>CL</sup> + γ<sub>k</sub>δ<sub>ij</sub><sup>RC</sup>. The layer coefficients γ<sub>k</sub> are multipliers showing how the [RC] association varies across layers (e.g., across countries or time periods), with one layer fixed at 1.0 as reference.
</div>

**9. Compared to general association models, models for ordinal variables provide:**

`r longmcq(c("Less statistical power",
             "More parameters to estimate",
             answer = "More focused tests with greater power and fewer degrees of freedom",
             "Only categorical interpretation"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
Models for ordinal variables give more focused tests → greater power to detect associations. They use fewer df → can fit different models between independence [A][B] and saturated [AB], have fewer parameters → easier interpretation and smaller standard errors. This is similar to using CMH tests or testing linear contrasts in ANOVA.
</div>

**10. When comparing multiple models using AIC and BIC, which statement is TRUE?**

`r longmcq(c("AIC and BIC always select the same model",
             "Lower values indicate worse fit",
             answer = "BIC penalizes complexity more heavily than AIC, often preferring simpler models",
             "Both criteria ignore degrees of freedom"))`

<div class="webex-solution">
<button>Explanation</button>
BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) penalizes model complexity more heavily than AIC (Akaike Information Criterion). BIC = -2*log-likelihood + log(n)*df, while AIC = -2*log-likelihood + 2*df. As a result, BIC often prefers more parsimonious models. Lower values of both criteria indicate better models, balancing goodness-of-fit against complexity.
</div>
